module_title: Finality, Revision Powers, and the Mandatory Deposit Rule
introduction: Tailored for advanced legal exams and Judiciary Mains, this level explores the post-judgment machinery of the SCC. It details why SCC decrees cannot be appealed, the expanded scope of 'Revision' under Section 25, and the draconian proviso of Section 17 that traps defendants seeking to set aside ex-parte orders.

core_concepts.title: Finality of Decrees (Section 27)
core_concepts.description:
The cornerstone of 'speedy justice'.
- The Rule: Save as provided by this Act, a decree or order made under the jurisdiction of a Court of Small Causes shall be **FINAL**.
- Implication: A losing party CANNOT file a regular First Appeal (under Section 96 of the CPC) against the judgment of a Small Cause Court. The regular appellate hierarchy is completely bypassed to prevent petty disputes from dragging on for decades.

core_concepts.title: The Power of Revision (Section 25)
core_concepts.description:
The only safeguard against a completely flawed SCC judgment.
- The Mechanism: Since there is no appeal, the aggrieved party can file a 'Revision' to the High Court (or to the District Judge, under specific State amendments like in UP).
- The Scope: The Revisional Court calls for the records to satisfy itself that a decree or order made in any case decided by a Court of Small Causes was **'according to law'**.
- Distinction from CPC Sec 115: Revision under Sec 25 of the SCC Act is WIDER than Revision under Sec 115 of the CPC. Under CPC, revision is strictly limited to 'jurisdictional errors'. Under the SCC Act, the High Court can interfere if the decision is simply 'not according to law' (e.g., misinterpretation of a statute).

core_concepts.title: The Draconian Proviso: Setting Aside Ex-Parte Decrees (Section 17)
core_concepts.description:
A highly tested, unique procedural hurdle.
- The Scenario: An SCC judge passes an ex-parte decree against a defendant who didn't show up. The defendant applies to set it aside (similar to Order 9 Rule 13 of CPC) or seeks a review.
- The Mandatory Proviso: The applicant MUST, at the time of presenting the application, either **deposit in the Court the exact amount due under the decree** or give security for the performance of the decree.
- Consequence of Failure: If the deposit or security is not given *at the time of making the application*, the application is inherently defective and will be dismissed immediately. This prevents defendants from using delay tactics to frustrate the winning plaintiff.

important_entities.name: State Amendments to Revision Jurisdiction
important_entities.key_fact: District Judges stepping into the High Court's shoes.
important_entities.significance: Under the central Act of 1887, Revision under Section 25 lies to the High Court. However, states like Uttar Pradesh drastically amended Section 25, directing that Revisions from the SCC shall lie to the **District Judge**, completely unburdening the High Court from petty monetary revisions.

trap_alerts_and_exceptions.explanation: Advanced exams pose this scenario: 'A defendant files an application to set aside an SCC ex-parte decree on Monday, but deposits the decretal amount on Friday. Is the application valid?' **NO**. The Supreme Court has strictly interpreted Section 17 Proviso: the deposit or the furnishing of security must be a condition precedent, done *at the time of presenting the application*, or the application is fundamentally invalid.

mnemonics_and_tricks.explanation: Remember these three words to summarize the entire operational flow of the Small Cause Courts Act.

exam_strategy_tips: In UP PCS-J Mains, if asked about challenging an SCC decree, you must clearly write that while a regular appeal is barred under Section 27, the aggrieved party has the remedy of **Revision to the District Judge under the UP Amendment to Section 25**, on the grounds that the decree was not 'according to law'.
